evidence_set: Gastrointestinal effects in 36 (51%): vomiting 31, nausea alone 5. Tachycardia in 27 (38%; no threshold stated) and systolic blood pressure above 140 mmHg in 32 (45%). Median stay 16 hours (IQR 11.3–24.4; range 1.8–228). Eight (11%), all of whom had taken tramadol with another medicine, went to intensive care: 5 for the other medicines' toxicity (tricyclic antidepressants 3, morphine 1, atenolol 1) and 3 for respiratory depression (one intubated, one on a naloxone infusion, one who developed pneumonia). No deaths. Naloxone was given to 9, seven with documented respiratory depression: it was reported to improve oxygen saturation or consciousness in 6, to improve them partly in 2 and to have no effect in 1; no seizures were reported after it.

The authors say serotonin toxicity reported after therapeutic use or overdose of tramadol has been with other medicines given with it, particularly serotonergic antidepressants (1st paragraph); later they say the majority of reported cases involved co-ingested serotonergic drugs and only one unusual severe case has been described (5th paragraph). Their concluding paragraph takes the absence of serotonin toxicity in these overdoses as suggesting that at therapeutic doses tramadol is unlikely to cause more than minor serotonergic effects, although nobody taking therapeutic doses, alone or with antidepressants, was studied.

Background: much of the toxicity in tramadol overdose is thought to be due to monoamine uptake inhibition rather than its opioid effects (citing Spiller et al., a prospective multicentre evaluation of tramadol exposures); and, citing a review of tramadol's clinical pharmacology, tramadol is metabolised by CYP2D6 to O-desmethyltramadol, a more potent μ-receptor agonist with a longer half-life (9 hours against 6 for tramadol), which contributes to tramadol's duration and analgesic potency.

evidence_set: Among people who used benzodiazepines, misuse rather than use as prescribed went with younger age (65 or older against 18–25, adjusted OR 0.23, 0.15–0.34), male gender (women 0.74, 0.61–0.90), tobacco (1.41), any alcohol (1.42) and alcohol abuse or dependence (2.31, 1.73–3.09), any marijuana (1.88) and marijuana abuse or dependence (2.39, 1.62–3.52), prescription opioid misuse (4.11, 3.26–5.18) and abuse or dependence (4.81, 3.45–6.72), and prescription stimulant misuse (2.46, 1.85–3.27) and abuse or dependence (3.40, 1.72–6.70); fair or poor self-rated health (0.61, 0.47–0.80) and prescription opioid use as prescribed (0.69, 0.57–0.84) went with lower odds, and prescription stimulant use as prescribed was not significantly associated (0.90, 0.74–1.09); heroin, mental illness, income, education and Medicaid were not associated.

evidence_set: 471 online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, the two sites earlier DIMS monitoring found most active on ecstasy tablets; collected by hand, with each report's stated content, physical description, picture and date archived. DIMS employees compared each report with DIMS database records (GC–MS composition, physical characteristics, date and place of submission) of the tablet within 12 weeks before or after the report's date. Stated MDMA was scored too high or too low if more than 10 mg from the database value (for a range, its average); 'unreported substance' if similar database tablets in the window held substances the report did not mention; 'dangerous' if stated more than 40 mg too low (for a range, its average 40 mg too low or its maximum 40 mg below the database maximum) or if an unreported substance was psychoactive and present in relevant concentrations (not defined in numbers). The comparison rested only on the report's own information, so a poorly described tablet matched several distinct database tablets ('multiple database hits'), which the authors take to mean that several pills on the market fitted the description and a reader could not tell them apart from the report. All four authors list the Trimbos Institute as an affiliation, and the scoring was done by DIMS employees; the paper does not state who runs DIMS.

The authors call this, to their knowledge, the first study of how reliable online information on ecstasy content is; they say people in the Netherlands are arguably better informed about drug content than elsewhere because of DIMS, and that extrapolating abroad needs care. They tried to score each report's source (experience, home test, laboratory test) and gave up: reports often named no source, and where DIMS laboratory tests were named as the source the stated amounts were frequently not found in the database (no numbers given). Declaration of interests: none.

evidence_set: National Poison Data System records of reports by members of the public and health-care providers to US poison centres, most commonly collected and coded by Specialists in Poison Information; forensic testing to confirm the reported exposure is not routinely performed. Retrieved: all intentional single-agent exposures to 11 designer benzodiazepines (adinazolam, clonazolam, cloniprazepam, diclazepam, etizolam, flubromazepam, flubromazolam, meclonazepam, nifoxipam, norflurazepam, pyrazolam), 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2017, all routes; accidental ingestions and exposures to more than one substance excluded. Etizolam had been tracked since 2007, but specific codes for all the other agents were added only in 2016; agents without a specific code could not be retrieved.

Table 3, the ten most common clinical effects and therapies among the 234: drowsiness/lethargy 152 (65%), slurred speech 40 (17%), confusion 32 (14%), agitated/irritable 22 (9%), ataxia 21 (9%), tachycardia 20 (9%), hypotension 19 (8%), coma 10 (4%), bradycardia 9 (4%); intubation 7 (3%), ventilator 5 (2%). The text gives agitation/irritability as 14% and coma as 8%, which do not match the table's counts for those effects (they are the percentages of the table's confusion and hypotension rows), and adds respiratory depression (3%), respiratory arrest (0.4%) and cardiac arrest (0.4%); 224 (95%) of the exposures were by ingestion.

evidence_set: A healthy 19-year-old man was referred to the authors (Stepping Hill Hospital, Stockport) with a 24-hour history of acute retention of urine; apart from a painful, palpable bladder, general examination and analysis of the urine showed nothing abnormal. A urethral catheter was inserted and removed after 36 hours on free drainage, and no further retention occurred (no length of follow-up given). He reported earlier amphetamine use and cannabis smoking, but only ecstasy in the 12 months before admission, one or two tablets once or twice a week, usually at parties, and later said he had taken 15 tablets in the 36 hours before admission. No drug screen of the man and no analysis of the tablets is reported (the urine analysis is not described as a drug test), and when the last tablet was taken is not stated.

The authors know of only one earlier urological complication of the drug, urgency of passing urine (citing Greer and Tolbert, 1986, not read). Their explanation is reasoning from the bladder's nerve supply, not a measurement: alpha-adrenergic fibres supply the trigone and bladder neck, stimulating them can produce bladder-neck dysfunction or closure, and MDMA is called a potent alpha-adrenergic agonist (no source given for this); they conclude that misuse of the drug almost certainly led to the retention in this case, recommend that use of synthetic amphetamines be considered in young people with unexplained retention, and cite an earlier report of bladder outflow obstruction after intravenous amphetamine (Worsley et al., 1989, not read). No residual volume, flow study, imaging, blood test or follow-up is reported. The photograph caption beside the item presents retention of urine as something large doses of ecstasy can cause, a general statement drawn from one case.
